title: Calculating PED and reading it off the curve

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Calculate PED from the percentage change in quantity demanded and the percentage change in price, classify the result as elastic, inelastic, unit elastic, perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic, and read elasticity off a demand curve diagram, including the vertical, horizontal and unit-elastic curves.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: The formula and its sign
blocks.text: PED equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. The raw answer comes out negative, because the law of demand makes the two changes run opposite ways; it is stated as an absolute value, the sign dropped by convention, and the size compared with 1. Worked case: Kaoko Juice sells 200 bottles a week at N$10 in Opuwo, raises the price to N$12, and sales fall to 150 bottles. The percentage change in quantity demanded is negative 25 per cent, since 50 / 200 x 100 = 25; the percentage change in price is positive 20 per cent, since 2 / 10 x 100 = 20. PED is 25 / 20 = 1.25, so demand is price-elastic: quantity demanded moved further, in percentage terms, than the price did.

blocks.heading: An inelastic case, worked
blocks.text: A minibus operator in Ruacana charges N$40 a trip and carries 500 passengers a month. The fare rises to N$60 and passengers fall to 460. Quantity demanded fell by 40, since 500 - 460 = 40, or 8 per cent of 500; price rose by N$20, or 50 per cent of N$40. PED is 8 / 50 = 0.16, and because 0.16 lies between 0 and 1 demand is price-inelastic: passengers cut back far less than the fare rose, in percentage terms.

blocks.heading: Reading elasticity off the diagram
blocks.text: On a demand diagram - price on the vertical axis, quantity demanded on the horizontal - elasticity is seen by comparing how far a point moves along each axis. A steeply drawn curve shows quantity demanded moving little for a given price move: inelastic demand, like the Ruacana trips. A flatter curve shows it moving far: elastic demand, like the juice. Steepness is judged in relation to the scales chosen, so the axis movement is the safer guide than the look of the line. And the whole range matters: a curve can hold an elastic stretch near high prices and an inelastic stretch near low ones.

blocks.heading: Three special values: 0, 1 and infinity
blocks.text:
Three values of PED have names of their own, and each has its own curve shape.

Perfectly inelastic demand, PED = 0. Quantity demanded does not change at all when the price changes, so the percentage change in quantity is zero and so is PED. The demand curve is a vertical line at that quantity: whatever the price, the same amount is bought. Few real goods come close, but a hospital that needs a fixed number of doses of a life-saving drug each week, whatever they cost, is near this case. Every rise in price then raises spending on the drug by the full percentage of the price rise, because no dose is dropped.

Perfectly elastic demand, PED = infinity. At one price buyers will take any quantity offered, but at any higher price quantity demanded falls to zero, because buyers can get an identical product elsewhere at that price. The demand curve is a horizontal line at that price. A grower near Grootfontein selling maize to a national mill that pays every grower N$5 000 a tonne is close to this case: he can sell as many tonnes as he grows at N$5 000, but if he asks N$5 100 the mill takes none of his maize.

Unit elasticity, PED = 1. The percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, so the two offset each other. The demand curve is drawn as a smooth curve that bends towards the origin, along which price multiplied by quantity is the same at every point: N$20 x 100 units, N$25 x 80 units and N$40 x 50 units each give N$2 000. The percentage formula, which measures each change from its own starting value, gives exactly 1 only for very small moves along this curve. Section 2.7.4 shows what unit elasticity means for spending.

These three mark out the scale. Between 0 and 1 demand is inelastic; above 1 it is elastic; and the vertical and horizontal lines are the two extremes between which real demand curves lie.
